# All-coordinate section variance for arbitrarily many opposite pairs

Let Y_1,Y'_1,...,Y_k,Y'_k be independent unit-rate exponentials, k>=1,
and let p_i>0. Additional independent unit-rate exponentials with zero
coefficient are permitted. Put

    V=sum_(i=1)^k p_i(Y_i-Y'_i),
    F=Pr(V>=0)=1/2,
    mu_j=E(Y_j|V=0),

where conditioning at zero means the actual coarea conditional law.
Then

    product_all_j mu_j>=1/4,
    product_(j!=r) mu_j>=1/4 for every r.           (1)

The full-product inequality is strict for k>=2. All omitted-coordinate
inequalities are then strict as well. No equality of the positive p_i
is imposed, and k is arbitrary.

For the uniform simplex whose vertex coefficients are
(p_1,...,p_k,-p_1,...,-p_k), with any zero coefficients appended, the
conditional means equal d times the barycentric section-centroid
coordinates. Thus (1) proves the desired cap-variance products in every
dimension for this opposite-paired class. It is not a claim about
unpaired phase patterns or arbitrary mixed-integer fibers.

## 1. Pair coordinates and conditional means

Set D_i=Y_i-Y'_i and M_i=min(Y_i,Y'_i). The change of variables on each
of the two half-planes has absolute Jacobian one, and its density is

    exp(-2M_i-|D_i|), M_i>=0, D_i in R.

Therefore M_i~Exp(2), D_i has density exp(-|t|)/2, and these variables
are independent. All pairs are independent. The event V=0 depends
only on the D_i, so the M_i retain their means 1/2 under conditioning.
The simultaneous symmetry D_i -> -D_i preserves this conditional law.
Consequently

    mu_i=mu'_i=1/2+(1/2)E(|D_i||V=0).             (2)

For k=1, D_1=0 under the section law and mu_1=mu'_1=1/2. This already
proves the full-product equality in that case. Additional zero-phase
means remain one by independence.

## 2. A conditional absolute difference never gains mean

Suppose k>=2. The random variable sum_(j!=i)p_jD_j has a continuous,
strictly positive, even density g_i that is nonincreasing on [0,infinity).
Here is an elementary justification of the monotonicity used. Each
scaled Laplace density is even and decreasing. A nonnegative even
decreasing function is an integral of indicators of centered intervals
by its level-set representation. The convolution of two such interval
indicators is the overlap length of two intervals whose centers are
separated by |t|; that overlap is nonincreasing in |t|. Tonelli's theorem
therefore proves that convolution preserves even monotonicity. Induction
applies to the finitely many scaled Laplace densities. Continuity and
strict positivity follow directly from convolution of the positive
Laplace densities; the case of a single remaining density is immediate.

The coarea conditional density of D_i is proportional to

    exp(-|t|)g_i(p_i t).

Hence |D_i| has the Exp(1) density tilted by the nonincreasing positive
function g_i(p_i t), t>=0. For independent Exp(1) variables T,T',

    2 Cov(T,g_i(p_iT))
      =E[(T-T')(g_i(p_iT)-g_i(p_iT'))]<=0.

It follows that E(|D_i||V=0)<=1 and thus mu_i<=1. The inequality is
strict: an integrable, positive, nonincreasing density cannot be constant
on the whole positive half-line, and the displayed covariance integrand
is strictly negative on a product set of positive measure. Also mu_i>1/2,
since the conditional D_i density is positive away from zero.

We have therefore proved, for every active pair when k>=2,

    1/2<mu_i=mu'_i<1.                              (3)

## 3. The exact half-unit deficit

Radial conditioning of 2k independent exponentials on the homogeneous
hyperplane V=0 gives a Gamma(2k-1,1) radial variable. Equivalently, scaling
the coarea integral at zero by a common rate s gives s^(-(2k-1)), and
differentiating at s=1 gives

    sum_(i=1)^k (mu_i+mu'_i)=2k-1.

Using pair equality, this becomes

    sum_(i=1)^k (1-mu_i)=1/2.                      (4)

Put delta_i=1-mu_i>=0. The elementary product inequality
product(1-delta_i)>=1-sum delta_i applies because the total deficit is
1/2. It can be proved successively by
(1-a)(1-b)=1-a-b+ab and induction. Therefore

    product_(i=1)^k mu_i>=1/2.

Squaring, and multiplying by the zero-phase means one, proves the first
inequality of (1). For k>=2 at least two deficits are strictly positive
by (3), so the product inequality is strict. Finally every individual
mean, including a zero-phase mean, is at most one. Removing any one
factor can only increase the full product, proving all other claims.

The symmetry that gives F=1/2 is the actual permutation swapping the
two members of every pair; V has a continuous density, so its zero event
has unconditional probability zero. All boundary and zero-coefficient
statements above use the conditional law directly, not a discarded
lower-dimensional measure.
